q: Which is the commonest epilepsy surgery procedure?
why: Anterior temporal lobectomy is the commonest.

q: During electrocorticography, which drug should be avoided because it suppresses epileptiform activity?
why: Avoid benzodiazepines and minimise volatile; alfentanil can activate epileptogenic foci to aid mapping.

q: How does long-term antiepileptic therapy affect non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers?
why: Enzyme induction causes relative resistance; monitor with train-of-four.

q: Which test is used to lateralise language and memory before epilepsy surgery?
why: The Wada (intracarotid amobarbital) test lateralises language and memory.

q: Why is delayed emergence common after epilepsy surgery?
o: Antiepileptic drugs, intra-op seizures, or complications such as haemorrhage
why: Consider continued AEDs, post-ictal state, haemorrhage and other causes of delayed emergence.

q: Which drug lowers seizure threshold and should be used with caution in epilepsy?
o: Some dopamine antagonists, xanthines and certain opioids
why: Be careful with drugs that lower the seizure threshold at emergence.

q: Which EEG pattern is typical of propofol anaesthesia on a spectrogram?
why: Propofol shows slow-delta plus coherent frontal alpha (8–12 Hz); ketamine shows high beta/low gamma (with theta); dexmedetomidine shows spindles (9–15 Hz) with slow/delta waves.

q: Which pattern on the spectrogram is typical of ketamine?
why: Ketamine produces high beta/low gamma activity with theta and gamma bursts.

q: A patient with epilepsy is on carbamazepine. What does this mean for other drugs?
o: It induces liver enzymes, speeding metabolism of many drugs
why: Carbamazepine and phenytoin are enzyme inducers.

q: After epilepsy surgery, what must be continued without interruption?
why: Continue antiepileptics and manage in neuro HDU.
